sections.title: Reading Passage — Acids and Bases at a Glance
body: An acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton acceptor, according to the Brønsted–Lowry definition. When an acid loses a proton, the species that remains is its conjugate base; when a base gains a proton, the product is its conjugate acid.

Water autoionizes: H2O(l) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + OH−(aq), with Kw = [H3O+][OH−] = 1.0 × 10−14 at 25 °C. This single constant lets us convert between hydronium and hydroxide concentrations in any aqueous solution.
pH = −log[H3O+] and pOH = −log[OH−]; at 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.00. Solutions with pH < 7 are acidic, pH > 7 are basic, and pH = 7 is neutral.

Strong acids (HCl, HNO3, H2SO4) ionize completely; weak acids (HF, CH3COOH, HCN) ionize only partially. The ionization constant Ka measures strength — larger Ka means a stronger acid. The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.
common_mistakes: Strength and concentration are different ideas: a dilute strong acid can have a higher pH than a concentrated weak acid.

items.q: Which species is the conjugate base of H2O?
items.explain: Removing a proton (H+) from H2O leaves OH−.

items.q: Which of the following is a Brønsted–Lowry acid in the reaction HCO3−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H2CO3(aq) + OH−(aq)?
items.answer: H2O (it donates a proton to HCO3−)
items.explain: H2O loses H+ to become OH−, so water is the acid.

items.q: Which species is amphiprotic?
items.answer: HSO4− (can donate OR accept a proton)
items.explain: OH− can only accept a proton; NH4+ can only donate; Cl− does neither.

items.q: At 25 °C, a solution has pH = 3.00. What is [H3O+]?
A solution has [OH−] = 1.0 × 10−9 M at 25 °C. What is its pH?
Which acid is the strongest?
items.explain: Larger Ka means more ionization, hence a stronger acid.

items.q: Kb for the conjugate base of a weak acid with Ka = 1.0 × 10−6 is:
Which statement about strong acids is TRUE?
choices: They have very small Ka values
items.explain: Complete ionization is the definition of a strong acid; concentration is a separate idea.

items.q: Pure water at 25 °C has:
items.explain: Autoionization produces equal amounts of both ions.

items.q: The pH of a solution changes from 4.00 to 5.00. The [H3O+] has:
items.explain: Each pH unit = a tenfold change; higher pH = lower [H3O+].

items.q: Calculate [H3O+] and [OH−] in pure water at 25 °C.
A solution has [H3O+] = 2.0 × 10−6 M. Find [OH−] and classify the solution.
Calculate the pH of 0.050 M HCl (ionizes completely).
Calculate the pOH and pH of 0.010 M NaOH.
What are [H3O+] and [OH−] when pH = 8.50?
A 0.10 M solution of a weak acid is 1.5% ionized. Calculate Ka.
Write the reaction of NH3 with water and label the acid, base, conjugate acid, and conjugate base.
items.answer: NH3(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ NH4+(aq) + OH−(aq). Acid: H2O · Base: NH3 · Conjugate acid: NH4+ · Conjugate base: OH−

items.q: Explain why the conjugate base of a weak acid is a stronger base than the conjugate base of a strong acid.
items.answer: The weaker the acid, the less it ionizes, so its conjugate base has a greater tendency to accept a proton back (Ka × Kb = Kw; smaller Ka → larger Kb).

items.q: A student says 'pH 2 is twice as acidic as pH 1.' Explain why this is wrong and give the correct relationship.
items.answer: pH is a log scale: pH 1 has [H3O+] = 10× that of pH 2, so pH 1 is TEN times more acidic, not twice.

items.q: Why is water called amphiprotic? Give one reaction showing water as an acid and one showing water as a base.
items.answer: Water can donate a proton (e.g., H2O + NH3 → NH4+ + OH−) and accept a proton (e.g., HCN + H2O → CN− + H3O+).
